answerSnippet: A healthy active-to-passive vocabulary ratio is between 0.40 and 0.60 (40–60%). Calculate it by dividing your active words (the ones you produce when speaking or writing) by your passive words (the ones you recognize when reading or listening). Below 40%, you need more production practice — speaking, writing, active recall. Above 60%, grow your passive base through extensive reading.
title: Active vs Passive Vocabulary Ratio Calculator + CEFR Table | Hacé Cuentas
h1: Active vs. Passive Vocabulary Ratio Calculator
description: Calculate your active-to-passive vocabulary ratio and check whether you're in the healthy 40–60% range. Includes full word-count tables by CEFR level: A1, A2, B1, B2, C1 and C2.
intro: Your **active vocabulary** is the set of words you can spontaneously produce when speaking or writing. Your **passive vocabulary** is the (much larger) set of words you recognize when reading or listening but don't yet produce fluently. Vocabulary acquisition research (Paul Nation, 2013; Laufer, 1998) shows that a learner's active vocabulary typically sits at **40–60%** of their passive vocabulary. This calculator divides your active word count by your passive word count and tells you whether your ratio is balanced — if it falls below 40%, you understand far more than you can produce, a sign you need more output practice (speaking, writing, active-recall flashcards). Rough CEFR benchmarks for active words: A1 ≈ 300–500, A2 ≈ 1,000–1,500, B1 ≈ 2,000–3,000, B2 ≈ 4,000–5,000, C1 ≈ 7,000–10,000 and C2 ≈ 15,000–20,000.
keyTakeaway: **Ratio = active words ÷ passive words.** An active/passive ratio between 0.40 and 0.60 is healthy (Nation, 2013). Below 0.40 you need more production practice; above 0.60, expand your passive base through extensive reading.
useCases: An intermediate English learner diagnosing whether their bottleneck is receptive or productive vocabulary before a Cambridge B2 exam.
A language teacher tracking students' progress: measuring the ratio at the start and end of a semester shows whether the method favors production.
A self-study learner with thousands of passive Anki cards (recognition) who wants to know what share has actually migrated to active use (production recall).
A learner of Spanish preparing for DELE B1 or B2 who needs to estimate how many more active words they still need.

example.title: Example: B1 English learner
steps: An English learner tracks 3,000 words in Anki that they can recall without seeing the translation (active vocabulary) and 7,000 words they recognize while reading but don't produce spontaneously (passive vocabulary).
Ratio = 3,000 ÷ 7,000 = 0.43 (43%). That's inside the healthy 40–60% range, near its lower edge.

Conclusion: the learner has a solid receptive base but should keep reinforcing speaking and writing so more words migrate from passive to active. Writing practice, shadowing and conversation will push the ratio up.

explanation:
## How It's Calculated

The formula is a direct division:

```
ratio = active_words ÷ passive_words
```

The result is a decimal between 0 and 1 (values above 1 are rare and usually indicate a counting error — you can't reliably produce more words than you recognize).

---

## Interpreting Your Active/Passive Ratio

| Ratio | Percentage | Diagnosis |
|---|---|---|
| < 0.30 | < 30% | Strong asymmetry: lots of input, little output. You urgently need production practice. |
| 0.30 – 0.39 | 30–39% | Below the healthy range. More speaking, writing and active recall. |
| 0.40 – 0.60 | 40–60% | Healthy range according to research (Nation, 2013). |
| 0.61 – 0.75 | 61–75% | Solid productive vocabulary. Read more extensively to grow your passive base. |
| > 0.75 | > 75% | Unusual. Double-check how you're counting passive words. |

---

## Text Coverage by Active Vocabulary Size (English)

| Active words | Coverage of general text | Approx. level |
|---|---|---|
| 500 | ~60% | A1–A2 |
| 1,000 | ~72% | A2 |
| 2,000 | ~80% | B1 |
| 3,000 | ~84% | B1–B2 |
| 5,000 | ~88% | B2 |
| 10,000 | ~92% | C1 |
| 20,000 | ~95% | C2 |

Source: Nation (2013), based on the British National Corpus.

---

## How to Estimate Your Active Word Count

- **Anki / SRS**: count the cards in production mode (you write or say the answer) that you pass consistently.
- **Frequency test**: tools like Paul Nation's Vocabulary Size Test measure passive coverage. Multiply by your estimated ratio to approximate the active count.
- **Writing sample**: write 500 words on a free topic and count the unique lemmas. It's a proxy for your real active vocabulary on that topic.

---

## Common Errors

1. **Confusing word tokens with word families.** Counting "run, runs, ran, running" as 4 words inflates your estimate 3–4×. All four belong to one word family. CEFR benchmarks use word *families*, not tokens.
2. **Equating passive and active vocabulary.** Recognizing a word while reading is not the same as producing it spontaneously. Passive vocabulary is 2–5× larger than active. CEFR speaking/writing tests measure active production.
3. **Counting cognates at face value.** A Spanish speaker learning Italian or Portuguese "inherits" hundreds of nearly-free passive words, which deflates the ratio without reflecting real learning effort. Exclude transparent cognates or track them separately.
4. **Treating the ratio as topic-independent.** Vocabulary is highly domain-dependent: you may sit at 60–70% in your professional field and 20% in cooking or medicine. Use the global ratio as a summary, and measure by domain to find concrete gaps.

---

## Limitations

The ratio is an indicator, not an exact measurement. Word counts from self-tracking (Anki decks, vocabulary tests) carry an error margin of ±1,000–2,000 words, and cognates in related languages artificially inflate the passive count.

faq.q: What is the difference between active and passive vocabulary?
faq.a: Active (productive) vocabulary consists of words you can spontaneously use when speaking or writing. Passive (receptive) vocabulary includes words you understand when reading or listening but may not produce on your own. Research consistently shows passive vocabulary is 2–5× larger than active vocabulary. For example, a solid B2 learner may have ~4,000–5,000 active words but recognize ~8,000–10,000 passively.

faq.q: What active/passive ratio is considered healthy?
faq.a: Second-language acquisition research (Nation, 2013; Laufer, 1998) suggests that a ratio between 0.40 and 0.60 (40–60%) is balanced for intermediate and advanced learners. Below 0.40 there is an imbalance typical of learners who read a lot but rarely practice speaking or writing. Above 0.60–0.75 your production is strong relative to your receptive base — a good moment to read extensively and grow passive vocabulary.

faq.q: How many active words do I need for each CEFR level?
faq.a: As a guideline: A1 ≈ 300–500, A2 ≈ 1,000–1,500, B1 ≈ 2,000–3,000, B2 ≈ 4,000–5,000, C1 ≈ 7,000–10,000 and C2 ≈ 15,000–20,000 active words. These values vary by language: in German, one root covers several compound forms; in English, Spanish cognates reduce the effort for Romance-language speakers.

faq.q: How many words does a native English speaker know?
faq.a: According to research by Nation (2006) and large-scale vocabulary tests (Brysbaert et al., 2016), average native adult English speakers command approximately 16,000–20,000 word families actively and recognize far more passively — roughly 2 to 3 times their active count. Half of that vocabulary is acquired before age 5, with the rest added at 1,000–2,000 words per year through adulthood.

faq.q: How can I grow my active vocabulary faster?
faq.a: The techniques with the strongest evidence are: (1) active-recall flashcards with spaced repetition (Anki in write/say-the-answer mode, not recognition only), (2) frequent free writing (journaling in the target language), (3) conversation with a native speaker or language exchange, and (4) shadowing for oral production. The key is forced output: the brain consolidates a word into active vocabulary when it must retrieve it without seeing it.

faq.q: Why can I understand almost everything but still struggle to speak?
faq.a: That's the classic symptom of a low active/passive ratio: most of your vocabulary is in receptive mode. Listening and reading grow passive vocabulary almost automatically with enough exposure, but a word only becomes active after being actively retrieved several times under time pressure (as in conversation). The fix is to reduce pure-input time and increase output with feedback.

faq.q: What is a 'word family' and why does it matter?
faq.a: A word family is a base word plus all its inflected and derived forms that share a core meaning. For example, *economy, economic, economical, economically, economist, economize* all belong to one family. CEFR vocabulary benchmarks and Nation's frequency lists are measured in word families, not individual tokens. Counting tokens instead of families inflates your apparent vocabulary by a factor of 3–4×.

faq.q: How much text do high-frequency words cover?
faq.a: In English, the 2,000 most frequent word families (the General Service List) cover about 80% of general prose. The next 3,000 (including the Academic Word List) raise coverage to roughly 90%. Mastering those lists in active mode is the highest-return investment per study hour.

faq.q: How do I estimate my passive vocabulary without a formal test?
faq.a: The most practical method is Paul Nation's Yes/No test: you see a list of about 100 words mixed with 10 invented ones and mark the ones you know. The proportion of real words marked (corrected for false alarms on the invented ones) estimates your coverage. Free online versions exist for English, French and Spanish. Multiplying that percentage by the size of the frequency dictionary gives an estimate of total passive vocabulary.

faq.q: Does the ratio change depending on the topic?
faq.a: Yes, significantly. Your active vocabulary in topics you practice often (e.g., technology or your profession) can reach 60–70% of your passive base, while in gastronomy or medicine it may drop to 20%. A global ratio is useful as a summary, but to diagnose concrete gaps it's better to measure by topic domain.
